facts.statement: Borealopelta was an extinct herbivorous ankylosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: Borealopelta (meaning 'northern shield') is an extinct genus of herbivorous nodosaurid ankylosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of what is today Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: The species B. markmitchelli was named in 2017 by Caleb Brown and colleagues.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, B. markmitchelli, named in 2017 by Caleb Brown and colleagues from a well-preserved specimen known as the Suncor nodosaur.

facts.statement: The fossil preserved armor in life position, keratin sheaths, skin, and stomach contents.
facts.quote: It preserved not only the armor (osteoderms) in their life positions, but also remains of their keratin sheaths, overlying skin, and stomach contents from the animal's last meal.

facts.statement: Melanosomes found in the fossil indicate the animal had a reddish-pink skin tone.
facts.quote: Melanosomes were also found that indicate the animal had a reddish pinkish skin tone.

facts.statement: The holotype was uncovered on March 21, 2011, at the Millennium Mine, 30 km north of Fort McMurray, Alberta.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen was uncovered on March 21, 2011, at the Millennium Mine, an oil sands mine 30 km north of Fort McMurray, Alberta, that is owned and operated by Suncor Energy.

facts.statement: The specimen was discovered by a miner named Shawn Funk.
facts.quote: It was discovered by a miner, Shawn Funk, who was digging in the bank and noticed the specimen.

facts.statement: The recovery process took fourteen days in total.
facts.quote: The process took fourteen days in total.

facts.statement: The species name markmitchelli honors technician Mark Mitchell, who spent six years preparing the fossil.
facts.quote: The species B. markmitchelli was named for him in recognition of his skilled work.

facts.statement: Borealopelta measured 5.5 meters long and weighed 1.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Borealopelta was a large dinosaur, measuring 5.5 m long and weighing 1.3 MT.

facts.statement: Borealopelta had a straight tail instead of a club and a pair of long shoulder spines shaped like bull horns.
facts.quote: It had a straight tail rather than a tail club, unlike any ankylosaurids, and from the shoulders protruded a pair of long spines, shaped like the horns of a bull.

facts.statement: Pigment study suggests Borealopelta had reddish-brown countershaded coloration for camouflage.
facts.quote: Study of the pigments present in remnants of skin and scales suggests that it might have had a reddish-brown coloration in life, with a countershaded pattern that was used for camouflage.

facts.statement: Borealopelta is classified within the family Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: Borealopelta was classified by Brown et al. within Nodosauridae.

facts.statement: Borealopelta had a flexible keratin layer up to 16 cm thick that could withstand forces over 125,000 joules per square meter.
facts.quote: Borealopelta possessed a removable, flexible keratin layer up to 16 centimetres (6.3 inches) over its bony armor, allowing it to survive forces of over 125,000 joules per square meter.

facts.statement: Stomach contents indicate that ferns were a major part of Borealopelta's diet.
facts.quote: Examination of the specimen's stomach contents indicates that ferns were a major part of the animal's diet.

facts.statement: Charcoal in the stomach contents suggests Borealopelta fed in an area recovering from a recent wildfire.
facts.quote: Roughly six percent of the stomach contents contained charcoal as well, leading to the conclusion that Borealopelta was feeding in an area that was experiencing regrowth after a recent wildfire.

facts.statement: Researchers inferred the animal died only a few hours after ingesting ferns in early or mid-summer.
facts.quote: Brown and colleagues inferred that the ferns themselves had been halfway through their growing season when ingested, suggesting that the Borealopelta individual ingested them in early or mid-summer, dying only a few hours afterward.

facts.statement: Borealopelta lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 110–112 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Suncor Borealopelta was preserved in the marine sandstones and shales of the Wabiskaw Member of the Clearwater Formation, which were laid down during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period, about 110–112 million years ago.

facts.statement: At the time, the region was covered by the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea.
facts.quote: At that time, the region was covered by the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea that stretched from the Arctic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, and the Wabiskaw sediments were being deposited in an offshore marine environment.

facts.statement: A siderite concretion formed around the carcass, preventing scavenging and preserving the body intact.
facts.quote: A siderite concretion began to form around the carcass shortly after its arrival on the seabed, which prevented scavenging and preserved the body intact, with its scales and osteoderms in their original configuration.

facts.statement: Borealopelta lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago in the Aptian age, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 125 millones de años, en la época del Aptiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica

facts.statement: The generic name Borealopelta derives from the Latin "borealis" meaning "north" and Greek "pelta" meaning "shield", referencing the northern locality and preserved osteoderms.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis placed Borealopelta in a clade with other nodosaurids, including Pawpawsaurus campbelli, Europelta carbonensis, and Hungarosaurus tormai as a sister taxon.
